title: King Al-Nu'man and the Faithful Bedouin
summary: King Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir of Al-Hirah had instituted two ceremonial days in his court: a Day of Grace, on which he enriched whoever appeared before him, and a Day of Wrath, ...
keywords: al-nu'uman and the arab of the banu tay
full_text:
King Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir of Al-Hirah had instituted two ceremonial days in his court: a Day of Grace, on which he enriched whoever appeared before him, and a Day of Wrath, on which the first stranger to cross his path was condemned to death.

On a Day of Wrath, an honest, impoverished Bedouin of the Banu Tayy, who knew nothing of the royal decree, walked into the palace grounds carrying two dead partridges to sell to the royal kitchens.

The king frowned with sorrow, for he had sworn an oath: 'Stranger, the law of my Day of Wrath condemns you to the scaffold! Ask whatever favor you desire before you perish.'

The Bedouin stood with calm dignity: 'O King, I have three infant daughters and an aged mother starving in the desert; I have debts unpaid. Grant me a reprieve of one single year to settle my affairs, and by the Creator of the heavens, I swear to return on this exact day to face your sword.'

The king asked: 'Who will stand as your surety with his life if you fail to return?'

A noble courtier named Qarad stood forward: 'I will be his surety, sire.'

A year passed. On the appointed Day of Wrath, the scaffold was prepared, and Qarad was led out to be executed in place of the absent Bedouin.

Just as the sword was raised, a horseman appeared running across the plain—it was the Bedouin, covered in dust, arriving on the exact hour!

Al-Nu'man was struck with awe: 'Why did you return to death?' The Bedouin replied: 'So that no man should ever say that fidelity has perished among the Arabs!'

The king turned to Qarad: 'And why did you vouch for him?' Qarad replied: 'So that none should say generosity has died!'

The king wept, threw down his sword, abolished the cruel Day of Wrath forever, and rewarded both noble men with royal honors.
moral: Desert fidelity to one’s sacred word inspires universal mercy and turns execution into celebration.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Al-Nu'uman and the Arab of the Banu Tay"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
